newsitem.title: UK: FORECAST-Overseas ops help to lift Vodafone.
newsitem.headline: FORECAST-Overseas ops help to lift Vodafone.

text.p: Vodafone Group Plc's profits are expected to receive a maiden boost from overseas operations when the company reports full year results on Tuesday. But a decline in the all-important revenue per subscriber figure is also forecast.

Experts have pencilled in year pre-tax profits of 525-543 million pounds, after a 25 million stg exceptional gain on disposals, compared with 475.1 million last year. Overseas interests are expected to boost operating profit by around 10-20 million stg.
Final dividend is forecast to rise to 4.8 from 4.01p.

Analysts expect foreign investments of the biggest of Britain's four mobile telephone operators to take up the reins of group earnings amid increasing competition at home. They also expect the value of these businesses to start being reflected in Vodafone's share price.
Lehman Brothers expects profit contributions from international arms to surge to 141 million stg in 1997/98, 224 million in 1998/99 and 279 million in 1999/2000.
"We believe that Vodafone shares offer 19 percent upside and a total return in excess of 20 percent over the next nine months," the broker said.

Lehman Brothers, which believes Vodafone's foreign investments will be worth 122p per Vodafone share -- or 3.72 billion stg -- by December, sets a share price target of 320p by the end of this year. Vodafone's shares were trading at around 270p on Friday, valuing the company at around 8.25 billion pounds.
The mobile telephone group has more than four million subscribers worldwide through 11 overseas investments.
Analysts say weaknesses in Australia and increasing competition in Hong Kong should be more than compensated for by strong competitive positions in Greece, South Africa, France and The Netherlands.

But Vodafone is still dependent on the UK for the lion's share of profits and revenues and here, growth has been slow. Although official mobile penetration is only around 12 percent, analysts see annual revenues per subscriber fall 8-11 percent to 440-431 stg from 481 stg.

The decline is a feature of most cellular markets, fuelled by the continued migration of customers from analogue onto digital networks, a change in the mix of subscribers towards fewer business users and amid expected price cuts to help kick-start the market.

An analyst at Deutsche Morgan Grenfell said he was looking for a "robust statement" from Vodafone about plans to grow its market share -- possibly by re-branding all service providers under the Vodafone name, on one computer, to facilitate a national marketing campaign.

"Once the migration issue is out of the way and they've gone through that exercise, they can probably focus a little bit more vigorously on growing the market without necessarily large tariff cuts," he said.

There has been no major change in UK cellular tariffs since the youngest mobile operator, Orange Plc, rolled out its network close to national coverage -- and other analysts warn the time is now ripe for a price war.
